narrative:
The model determined that you have an 87% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants students who are very likely to pass, this prediction led to the rejection of your application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. While accepted students typically rank around the middle of their class in year three, you placed in the bottom decile, a significant gap that heavily signaled risk to the model.

Next, your decision to attend law school part-time also worked against you. The vast majority of accepted students—nearly 93%—plan to study full-time. Part-time enrollment pulled the prediction further toward failure, as it is strongly associated with lower first-time bar passage rates.

Your first-year class ranking contributed as the third most important factor, again in the direction of failure. At the third decile, you ranked well below the average of accepted students, who tend to place around the sixth decile.

Taken together, these academic performance signals and your part-time status created a clear picture for the model. To improve your chances, focus on raising your grades if you retake courses, consider full-time study if possible, and look for post-baccalaureate programs that can strengthen your academic record before reapplying.
